SECTION 202 of Ajmer Tenancy and Land Records Act, 1950
202. Mode of service of summons or notice.-
(1) A summons issued by a court acting under this Act shall, if practicable, be served (a) personally on the person to whom it is addressed, or failing him on (b) hisauthorised agent or (c) an adult male member of his family who is residing with him.
(2) If service cannot be so made, or if any person mentioned in sub-section (1) refuses to accept service, the summons may be served by posting a copy thereof at the usual or last known place of residence of the person to whom it is addressed, or, if that person does not reside in the tahsil in which such court is held, and the case to which the summons relates has reference to land in that tahsil, then by posting a copy of the summons on some conspicuous place in or near the estate wherein the land is situated.
(3) If the summons relates to a case in which persons having the same interest are so numerous that personal service on all of them is not reasonably practicable, it may, if the court so directs, be served by delivery of a copy thereof to such of those persons as the court nominates in this behalf and by proclamation or publication in a local paper of the contents thereof for the information of the other persons interested in such case.
(4) A summons may, if the court so directs, be served on the person named therein, either in addition to, or in substitution for, any other mode of service, by forwarding the summons by post in a letter addressed to such person under a certificate of posting.
(5) When a summons is served in accordance with the provisions of this section, it shall be deemed to have been duly served.
(6) For the purposes of this section "summons" shall include a "notice" which a court may issue under this Act.
simplified_text:
Simplified text: Mode of Service of Summons or Notice:
1. The court must try to personally serve a summons to the intended person. If not possible, it can be served to the person's authorized agent or an adult male family member living with them.
2. If personal service is not feasible or refused, the summons may be posted at the person's usual or last-known residence. If the person does not reside in the same area as the court but the case is about land in that area, the summons can be posted in a visible location near the land.
3. If there are many people with the same interest in a case and personal service is impractical, the court may direct delivery to nominated persons and publish the contents in a local paper for others to know.
4. The court may also choose to send the summons by post, alongside any other method directed by the court.
5. When a summons is served as described above, it is considered properly served.
6. The term "summons" in this section includes any "notice" that the court may issue under this Act.

Power to Make Rules:
The Chief Commissioner has the authority to create rules to implement the Ajmer Tenancy and Land Records Act, 1950. These rules can cover various matters, including but not limited to:

Demarcating pasture land and private marking.
Attesting leases and agreements.
Collecting and distributing cesses, assessing and recovering irrigation dues, and resolving disputes related to them.
Training patwaris and girdawars.
Regulating the hiring and transferring of girdawars, patwaris, and other necessary staff for maintaining land records, including their salaries, qualifications, duties, leaves, dismissals, etc.
Specifying the format, contents, preparation methods, attestation, and maintenance of records like record-of-rights, annual registers, maps, field-books, and other relevant documents needed under this Act.
Setting up boundary and survey markers, maintaining, repairing, and renewing them, and recovering costs for these activities.
Determining principles for ejecting a tenant from a section of the land and demarcating that portion.
Recording transfers and changes affecting land interests, whether ownership or other forms of interest.
Regulating fines for not reporting succession or transfers.
Appointing lambardars and patels, defining their duties, possible remuneration, removal, and dismissals.
Establishing mechanisms for appeals and seeking redress for punishments given to employees involved in land records management.
Guiding officials on rent determination, enhancement, reduction, and commutation cases.
Guiding record officers and rent-rate officers.
Remitting or suspending rent and revenue during agricultural crises.
Defining the authority of various officials and revenue courts to handle cases.
Setting up honorary courts and village punchayats and regulating their functions.
Collecting fines, compensation, damages, or other payments imposed by the Act or its rules.
Levying fees for any application or relief under the Act where no specific provision exists.

Penalties:
Contravening any rule can lead to a fine of up to fifty rupees.
All rules made under this Act will be published in the Official Gazette and presented to Parliament soon after publication.

SECTION 204 of Ajmer Tenancy and Land Records Act, 1950
Chapter XVII
Transitional Provisions
204. Reinstatement of tenant ejected before commencement of this Act.-

Simplified text: Vice-Chancellor Duties at Aligarh Muslim University

Appointment and Role:
The Vice-Chancellor is appointed by the Visitor following procedures outlined in the Statutes. The Vice-Chancellor serves as the chief executive and academic officer of the University, overseeing and managing the University's activities and implementing decisions made by the University authorities.

Exercise of Powers:
If the Vice-Chancellor believes immediate action is necessary on any matter, they can use the powers delegated to any University authority under this Act. The Vice-Chancellor must report such actions to the respective authority. However, if the authority disagrees with the action, it can refer the matter to the Visitor for a final decision. Furthermore, any University staff member affected by the Vice-Chancellor's action has the right to appeal to the Executive Council within three months of being informed about the decision. The Executive Council has the authority to confirm, modify, or reverse the Vice-Chancellor's action.

Additional Powers:
In addition to these responsibilities, the Vice-Chancellor also carries out other duties and exercises additional powers as specified in the Statutes or Ordinances.

Simplified text: The University's Governing Body

Composition: The Court is made up of the Chancellor, Pro-Chancellor, Vice-Chancellor, Pro-Vice-Chancellor (if any), and other individuals specified in the Statutes.

Authority: The Court serves as the highest governing body of the University, with the power to exercise all University powers not specifically outlined in this Act, Statutes, Ordinances, or Regulations. It can review the actions of the Executive and Academic Councils, except when these councils have acted within their prescribed authority.

Powers and Duties: The Court has the following responsibilities:
- Formulating and adjusting Statutes
- Reviewing Ordinances
- Reviewing and approving the annual report, financial accounts, and budget estimates
- Appointing individuals to university bodies and roles outlined in the Act or Statutes
- Exercising any other powers or duties assigned by the Act or Statutes.

The setup, authority, and roles of the University's governing bodies and any new bodies created in the future.
The process of electing and retaining members of these bodies, filling vacant positions, and other related matters.
How the Chancellor, Pro-Chancellor, Vice-Chancellor, and other officials are selected or appointed.
The process of hiring teachers and other academic staff, as well as determining their pay.
The process of hiring non-academic staff and determining their pay.
Hiring visiting teachers or academic staff from other institutions for joint projects.
Employee conditions such as pension, insurance, provident fund, termination procedures, and disciplinary actions.
Rules for determining employee seniority.
The arbitration procedure for resolving employee or student disputes with the University.
The process for employees or students to appeal to the Executive Council regarding actions by University officials.
The recognition and establishment of student unions or associations for teachers, academic staff, or other employees.
Any other matters required by the Act that can be addressed in the Statutes.

- The AICTE is a legal entity with ongoing existence and the ability to enter into contracts and engage in legal proceedings.
- The Council's main office is in Delhi, with potential branch offices in other parts of India as approved by the Central Government.
- The Council's membership includes various appointed officials and representatives from government bodies, educational institutions, industry, and other relevant sectors.

Appointment of Council Members:
- The Council consists of members such as a Chairman and Vice-Chairman appointed by the Central Government.
- Ex officio members include officials from the Ministry of Government of India handling education, regional committee chairpersons, and heads of various educational boards.
- Members representing government ministries, state governments, industry, professional bodies, and other relevant organizations are appointed on a rotating basis according to set criteria.
- Certain key officials like the Chairman of the University Grants Commission and directors of research institutes are also ex officio members.

Recruitment and Service Conditions:

Simplified text: Declaring Ancient Monuments as National Importance

1. National Importance Declaration:
If the Central Government believes that an ancient monument or archaeological site not listed in Section 3 is significant to the nation, it can announce its intention to declare it as of national importance in the official Gazette. The notice is posted near the monument or site for two months.
2. Objections:
Within two months after the notice, anyone with an interest in the monument or site can object to its declaration as of national importance.
3. Final Declaration:
After the two-month period, considering any objections received, the Central Government can officially declare the monument or site as of national importance through a Gazette notification.
4. Conclusive Evidence:
Once published, the notification is considered conclusive proof that the monument or site is of national importance under this Act, unless withdrawn.

SECTION 4 of Ancient Monuments Preservation Act, 1904
4. Acquisition of rights in or guardianship of an ancientmonument.
(1)The Collector, with the sanction of the1[Central Government], may purchase or take a lease of any protected monument.
(2) The Collector, with the like sanction, may accept a gift or bequest of any protected monument.

(4) When the Commissioner has accepted the guardianship of a monument undersub-section(3), the owner shall, except as expressly provided in this Act, have the same estate, right, title and interest in and to the monument as if the Commissioner had not been constituted guardian thereof.
(5) When the Commissioner has accepted the guardianship of a monument undersub-section(3), the provisions of this Act relating to agreements executed under section 5 shall apply to the written instrument executed under the saidsub-section.

Simplified text: Acquisition and Protection of Ancient Monuments:

Purchase or Lease: With approval from the Central Government, the Collector can buy or lease an ancient monument that is protected.

Gifts and Bequests: With the same approval, the Collector can accept gifts or inheritances of protected monuments.

Guardianship: The owner of a protected monument can appoint the Commissioner as the guardian through a written document. The Commissioner, with approval from the Central Government, can accept this responsibility.

Rights of Ownership: If the Commissioner becomes the guardian, the owner still retains most ownership rights as if the Commissioner wasn't the guardian, unless this Act states otherwise.

Procedures: The rules for agreements made under section 5 apply to the written document appointing the Commissioner as guardian.

Monuments without Owners: If a protected monument has no owner, the Commissioner can take on the role of guardian.

Simplified text: Preservation Agreements for Ancient Monuments:

Proposing Agreement: The Collector, with approval from the Central Government, can suggest to the owner to enter into an agreement with the Central Government for preserving a protected ancient monument in the owner's district.

Contents of Agreement: The agreement may cover various aspects such as:
- Maintenance and care of the monument.
- Supervision of the monument and duties of any assigned personnel.
- Limitations on the owner's rights to make changes to the monument or the surrounding area.
- Access provided to the public or authorized individuals for inspection and upkeep.
- Notification required if the owner intends to sell the land where the monument is located, along with the Central Government's right to purchase at market value.
- Reimbursement of expenses related to the monument's preservation.
- Transfer of certain rights to the Government concerning the monument after incurring preservation expenses.
- Selection of an authority to resolve any disputes arising from the agreement.
- Any other relevant matters linked to the preservation of the monument that both parties agree on.

Modifying Agreement: The terms of the agreement can be adjusted over time with approval from the Central Government and the owner's consent.

Termination of Agreement: The Collector can end the agreement with a six-month written notice to the owner under the Central Government's approval. Similarly, the owner can terminate the agreement by giving a six-month notice to the Collector.

Binding Nature: The agreement is binding on any subsequent owners of the monument involved in the agreement.

Protection of Rights: Any rights obtained by the Central Government related to preservation expenses will remain unaffected even if the agreement is terminated.

Any disagreements about financial matters will be resolved through mutual agreement or by a decision made by the Central Government with advice from the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India.

The Andhra Pradesh reorganization Act, 2014

to the other provisions of this Part, all land and all stores, articles and

Land and Goods Transfer:

- If the Central Government decides certain goods should be distributed differently, they can issue directions for a fair distribution of those goods among Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.

- "Goods" excludes coins, bank notes, and currency notes.

SECTION 49 of Andhra Pradesh Reorganization Act, 2014
The Andhra Pradesh reorganization Act, 2014
49.  Treasury and bank balances.
The total of the cash balances in all treasuries of the existing

State of Andhra Pradesh and the credit balances of the existing State of Andhra

Pradesh with the Reserve Bank of India, the State Bank of India or any other

bank immediately before the appointed day shall be divided between the States

of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana on the basis of population ratio:
Provided that for the purposes of such division, there shall be

no transfer of cash balances from any treasury to any other treasury and the

apportionment shall be effected by adjusting the credit balances of the two

States in the books of the Reserve Bank of India on the appointed day:
Provided further that if the State of Telangana has no account

on the appointed day with the Reserve Bank of India, the adjustment shall be

made in such manner as the Central Government may, by order, direct.
simplified_text:
Simplified text: Division of Cash Balances:
According to Section 49 of the Andhra Pradesh Reorganization Act, 2014, upon the appointed day, the total cash balances in all treasuries and credit balances in banks belonging to the existing State of Andhra Pradesh will be shared between the States of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana based on their respective populations.
The division will be done without physically moving cash between treasuries. Instead, adjustments will be made to credit balances in the books of the Reserve Bank of India. If the State of Telangana does not have an account with the Reserve Bank of India on the appointed day, the Central Government will determine the adjustment process.

Simplified text: Investments and Credits Allocation:

Investment Distribution:
- Securities acquired using funds from the Cash Balances Investment Account or any Fund in the Public Account of the existing State of Andhra Pradesh, as listed in the Seventh Schedule, will be divided based on the population ratio of the successor states.
- Securities purchased from the Calamity Relief Fund of the existing State of Andhra Pradesh will be divided based on the territories occupied by the successor states.

Special Funds:
- Investments from the existing State of Andhra Pradesh in any special fund dedicated to a specific local area will be transferred to the state where that area is located on the appointed day. Private Undertakings:
- Investments from the existing State of Andhra Pradesh in private, commercial, or industrial entities confined to a specific local area will be transferred to the successor state encompassing the area on the appointed day. Inter-State Bodies:
- Investments, loans, or advances made by the existing State of Andhra Pradesh to a body corporate that became an inter-State entity under Part II will be shared between Andhra Pradesh and Telangana in the same proportion as the division of assets of the body corporate under this Act, unless specified otherwise.

undertakings.

Simplified text: Transfer of Assets and Liabilities:

Assets and liabilities of State Undertakings:
The assets and debts of any business or industry in the current state of Andhra Pradesh that operates solely within a specific local area will shift to the state where that area is located on the appointed day. This is regardless of where the main office is situated. However, if the business starts operating across states because of Part II, the assets and debts should be divided as follows:
The assets and debts of the operational sections should be shared between the two states based on their locations.
The main office's assets and debts should be divided between the states according to the population ratio.
After sharing assets and debts, they can be transferred physically upon mutual agreement or through payment or another method both states agree upon.

Public Debt Division:
- All debts and accounts of Andhra Pradesh before the restructuring will be distributed based on the population ratio of the new states, unless stated otherwise in this Act.

simplified_text:
Simplified text: Refund of Excessive Taxes
1. The responsibility to refund any excess tax or duty on property, such as land revenue, collected by the current State of Andhra Pradesh falls on the successor state where the property is located. The state handling the refund is entitled to its share from the other state.

The excess tax or duty will be divided between the successor states of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana based on their population ratios. The state in charge of refunding the excess payment is entitled to receive its share from the other state.

Simplified text: Deposits and Fund Allocation:

As of the designated day, any civil deposits or local fund deposits held by the current Andhra Pradesh state will become the responsibility of the new respective state where the deposit was made.

Charitable endowments will also become the responsibility of the new state where the institution or beneficiaries are located. In cases where the endowment's objectives are set within a specific state, responsibility will lie with that corresponding new state.

In situations where civil deposits, loan funds, or charitable endowments were managed by the prior Andhra Pradesh state covering the entire region, these funds will be divided between the new successor states based on their respective population ratios.

Before the appointed day, if the existing State of Andhra Pradesh has entered into any contracts using its executive power, the following rules apply:
If the contract is exclusively for the purposes of either Andhra Pradesh or Telangana after the appointed day, the state responsible for those purposes will handle the contract and its liabilities.
If the contract doesn't fall under the above condition, any rights and liabilities from the contract will be divided between Andhra Pradesh and Telangana based on population ratio or any other agreed method.

SECTION 66 of Andhra Pradesh Reorganization Act, 2014
The Andhra Pradesh reorganization Act, 2014

allocation or adjustment in certain cases.

of the successor States of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana becomes entitled to any

property or obtains any benefits or becomes subject to any liability, and the

Power to Allocate or Adjust Benefits:
If either Andhra Pradesh or Telangana gains property, benefits, or liabilities due to the reorganization, and one state feels it's fair to share with the other, they can ask the Central Government to decide.

Within three years of the reorganization, if one state requests and the Central Government agrees, the property or benefits will be divided between the states, or the other state will contribute to the shared liabilities. The decision will be made after consulting both state governments.

generation and supply of electric power and supply of water.

If the Central Government believes that changes to how electric power or water is generated or supplied in an area might harm that area due to it falling outside the State where the infrastructure is located, the Central Government can consult with the relevant State Governments and give directions to maintain the existing arrangements as much as possible. SECTION 70 of Andhra Pradesh Reorganization Act, 2014
The Andhra Pradesh reorganization Act, 2014
70.  Provisions as to Andhra Pradesh State

Financial Corporation.
1.    The

Andhra Pradesh State Financial Corporation established under the State

Financial Corporations Act, 1951 shall, on and from the appointed day, continue

to function in those areas in respect of which it was functioning immediately

before that day, subject to the provisions of this section and to such

directions as may, from time to time, be issued by the Central Government.
2.    Any

directions issued by the Central Government under sub-section ( 1 ) in

respect of the Corporation may include a direction that the said Act, in its

application to the Corporation, shall have effect subject to such exceptions

and modifications as may be specified in the direction.
3.    Notwithstanding

anything contained in sub-section ( 1 ) or sub-section ( 2 ), the

Board of Directors of the Corporation may, with the previous approval of the

Central Government and shall, if so required by the Central Government, convene

at any time after the appointed day a meeting for the consideration of a scheme

for the reconstitution or reorganisation or dissolution, as the case may be, of

the Corporation, including proposals regarding the formation of new

Corporations, and the transfer thereto of the assets, rights and liabilities of

the existing Corporation, and if such a scheme is approved at the general

meeting by a resolution passed by a majority of the shareholders present and

voting, the scheme shall be submitted to the Central Government for its

sanction. 
4.    If the

scheme is sanctioned by the Central Government either without modifications or

with modifications which are approved at a general meeting, the Central

Government shall certify the scheme, and upon such certification, the scheme

shall, notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in any law for the

time being in force, be binding on the Corporations affected by the scheme as

well as the shareholders and creditors thereof. 
5.    If the

scheme is not so approved or sanctioned, the Central Government may refer the

scheme to such Judge of the High Court of Andhra Pradesh or the High Court of

Telangana as may be nominated in this behalf by the Chief Justice thereof, and

the decision of the Judge in regard to the scheme shall be final and shall be

binding on the Corporations affected by the scheme as well as the shareholders

and creditors thereof. 
6.    Nothing

in the preceding provisions of this section shall be construed as preventing

the Government of the States of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana from constituting,

at any time on or after the appointed day, a State Financial Corporation for

that State under the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951.
simplified_text:
Simplified text: Provisions for Andhra Pradesh State Financial Corporation under the Andhra Pradesh Reorganization Act, 2014:

Continuation of Operations: The Andhra Pradesh State Financial Corporation, established under the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951, will continue its operations as before the appointed day, subject to specific provisions of this section and any directions given by the Central Government.

Central Government Directions: The Central Government may issue directions concerning the Corporation, including specifying exceptions and modifications to the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951 as it applies to the Corporation.

Board of Directors' Authority: The Board of Directors can convene a meeting, with prior Central Government approval, to discuss schemes for reconstitution, reorganization, or dissolution of the Corporation. If approved at a general meeting and by the Central Government, the scheme becomes binding.

Scheme Certification: If the scheme is approved by the Central Government, it will be certified and binding on the affected Corporations, shareholders, and creditors.

Judicial Review: If the scheme is not approved, it may be referred to a nominated High Court Judge for a final decision, which will be binding.

State Government Authority: The States of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana retain the right to establish a State Financial Corporation under the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951, at any time following the appointed day.

The Andhra Pradesh reorganization Act, 2014
73.  Special provisions relating to,

retrenchment compensation in certain cases.
Where on account of the reorganisation of the  existing State of

Andhra Pradesh under this Act, any body corporate constituted under a Central

Act, State Act or Provincial Act, any co-operative society registered under any

law relating to co-operative societies or any commercial or industrial

undertaking of that State is reconstituted or reorganised in any manner

whatsoever or is amalgamated with any other body corporate, co-operative

society or undertaking, or is dissolved, and in consequence of such

reconstitution, reorganisation, amalgamation or dissolution, any workman

employed by such body corporate or in any such co-operative society or

undertaking, is transferred to, or re-employed by, any other body corporate, or

in any other co-operative society or undertaking, then, notwithstanding

anything contained in section 25F or section 25FF or section 25FFF of the

Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, such transfer or re-employment shall not entitle

him to any compensation under that section:
Provided that-
a.    the

terms and conditions of service applicable to the workman after such transfer

or re-employment are not less favourable to the workman than those applicable

to him immediately before the transfer or re-employment;
b.    the

employer in relation to the body corporate, the co-operative society or the

undertaking where the workman transferred or re-employed is, by agreement or

otherwise, legally liable to pay to the workman, in the event of his

retrenchment, compensation under section 25F or section 25FF or section 25FFF

of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 on the basis that his service has been

continuous and has not been interrupted by the transfer or re-employment.

The new terms and conditions of the worker's employment should be at least as good as those before the transfer.
The employer must be legally responsible for providing compensation for retrenchment if the worker is let go, based on continuous service without interruption.

SECTION 74 of Andhra Pradesh Reorganization Act, 2014
The Andhra Pradesh reorganization Act, 2014
74.  Special provision as to income-tax.
Where the assets, rights and liabilities of any body corporate

carrying on business are, under the provisions of this Part, transferred to any

other bodies corporate which after the transfer carry on the same business, the

losses or profits or gains sustained by the body corporate first-mentioned

which, but for such transfer, would have been allowed to be carried forward and

set off in accordance with the provisions of Chapter VI of the Income-tax Act,

1961, shall be apportioned amongst the transferee bodies corporate in

accordance with the rules to be made by the Central Government in this behalf

and, upon such apportionment, the share of loss allotted to each transferee

body corporate shall be dealt with in accordance with the provisions of Chapter

VI of the said Act, as if the transferee body corporate had itself sustained

such loss in a business carried on by it in the years in which those losses

were sustained.

Simplified text: Special Tax Rule for Corporate Transfers:

If a body corporate's assets, rights, and liabilities are transferred to another body corporate under this Act and both continue the same business, any profits or losses that could have been carried forward for tax purposes will be shared among the new entities according to government rules. Each new entity will handle their share of losses as if they had incurred them in their own business operations.

Every employee who was working for the state of Andhra Pradesh before the specified day will continue working for Andhra Pradesh unless instructed otherwise by the Central Government and in consultation with the successor states.
After the specified day, the Central Government will assign each employee to a successor state based on their preference, with adjustments made as necessary. Simplified text: Other Provisions Regarding Services:

This section of the Andhra Pradesh Reorganization Act, 2014 clarifies the following points regarding services:

Applicable Constitution: The provisions of this section, as well as section 77, do not impact the operation of the Constitution's Chapter I of Part XIV concerning the terms of service for individuals working in Union or State affairs. However, any individual deemed to be allocated to the States of Andhra Pradesh or Telangana under section 77 cannot have their existing conditions of service changed to their disadvantage without prior approval from the Central Government.

Service Allocation: Any services provided by an individual before the "appointed day" will be considered as follows:
- If allocated to a specific State under section 77, their services will be viewed in connection with that State.
- If allocated to the Union for the administration of Telangana's successor State, their services will be considered in connection with the Union as per the applicable service rules.

All-India Service Members: Members of any All-India Service are not covered under the provisions of section 77.

Establishment of Council: On a specified day, the Central Government will create an Apex Council to oversee the operations of the Godavari River Management Board and Krishna River Management Board.

Simplified text: Creation and Role of River Management Boards

The Andhra Pradesh Reorganization Act, 2014 establishes River Management Boards for the Godavari and Krishna rivers to oversee, regulate, maintain, and operate identified projects. Key points include:

Board Establishment: Two separate boards, the Godavari River Management Board and Krishna River Management Board, are to be formed by the Central Government within sixty days from the designated commencement date. These boards will manage projects specified by the Central Government.

Board Structure: Each board will be led by a Chairperson appointed by the Central Government, along with members nominated by the successor states and experts designated by the Central Government. Additionally, each board will have a full-time Member Secretary from the Central Water Commission.

Board Functions: The boards, as autonomous bodies under Central Government control, will carry out various functions such as regulating water supply to the successor states in compliance with relevant agreements and awards, overseeing power distribution, and approving new water resource development projects. Additional responsibilities may be assigned by the Central Government in alignment with specified principles.

The Management Board must hire staff as needed to carry out its duties under this Act. Initially, staff should be deputed equally from the successor States and then permanently absorbed into the Board.

(4) For the removal of doubts, it is hereby declared that the mortgagee of any property referred to in sub-section (3) or any other person holding any charge, lien or other interest in, or in relation to, any such property shall be entitled to claim, in accordance with his rights and interests, payment of the mortgage money or other dues, in whole or in part, out of the amount specified in section 7 and also out of the amounts determined under section 8, but no such mortgage, charge, lien or other interest shall be enforceable against any property which has vested in this Central Government.
(5) Any licence or other instrument granted to the Company in relation to any undertaking which has vested in the Central Government under section 3 at any time before the appointed day and in force immediately before that day shall continue to be in force on and after such day in accordance with its tenor in relation to and for the purposes of such undertaking, and, on and from the date of vesting of such undertaking under section 6 in a Government company, such Government company shall be deemed to be substituted in such licence or other instrument as if such licence or other instrument had been granted to such Government company and that Government company shall hold it for the remainder of the period for which the Company would have held it under the terms thereof.
(6) If, on the appointed day, any suit, appeal or other proceeding of whatever nature in relation to any property which has vested in the Central Government, under section 3, instituted or preferred by or against the Company, is pending, the same shall not abate, be discontinued or be, in any way, prejudicially affected by reason of the transfer of the undertakings of the Company or of anything contained in this Act, but the suit, appeal or other proceeding may be continued, prosecuted or enforced by or against the Central Government, or, where the undertakings of the Company are directed, under section 6, to vest in a Government company, by or against the Government company.

SECTION 28 of Andhra Scientific Company Limited (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1982
28. Offences by companies.-
(1) Where an offence under this Act has been committed by a company, every person who, at the time the offence was committed was in charge of, and was responsible to, the company for the conduct of the business of the company, as well as the company, shall be deemed to be guilty of the offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly: Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall render any such person liable to any punishment, if he proves that the offence was committed without his knowledge or that he had exercised all due diligence to prevent the commission of such offence.
(2) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), where any offence under this Act has been committed by a company and it is proved that the offence has been committed with the consent or connivance of, or is attributable to any neglect on the part of, any director, manager, secretary or other officer of the company, such director, manager, secretary or other officer shall be deemed to be guilty of that offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly.
Explanation.-For the purposes of this section,-
(a) "company" means any body corporate and includes a firm or other association of individuals; and
(b) "director", in relation to a firm, means a partner in the firm.

SECTION 28 of Andhra State Act, 1953
Part IV
High Courts
28. High Court for Andhra.-
(1) As from the 1st day of January, 1956, or such earlier date as may be appointed under sub-section (2), there shall be a separate High Court for the State of Andhra (hereinafter referred to as "the High Court of Andhra").
(2) The President may, if a resolution recommending the establishment of a separate High Court for the State of Andhra has, after having been adopted by the Legislative Assembly of that State, been submitted to him, appoint, by notifications in the Official Gazette, a date earlier than the 1st day of January, 1956, for the purpose of sub-section (1).
(3) The date mentioned in sub-section (1) or, if an earlier date is appointed under subsection (2), the date so appointed is hereinafter referred to as the "prescribed day."
(4) The principal seat of the High Court of Andhra shall be at such place as the Governor of Andhra may, before the prescribed day, by order, appoint: Provided that if a resolution recommending any place for such principal seat is adopted by the Legislative Assembly of Andhra, such place shall be appointed by the Governor as the principal Seat.

Simplified text: Establishing the High Court for Andhra State:

Effective Date: Starting from January 1, 1956, or an earlier date chosen as per sub-section (2), a distinct High Court will be set up for Andhra State (referred to as "High Court of Andhra").

Appointment of a High Court: If the Legislative Assembly of Andhra State passes a resolution recommending the establishment of a separate High Court for the state, the President can appoint an earlier date than January 1, 1956, through official notifications in the Gazette as per sub-section (1).

Prescribed Day: The date mentioned in sub-section (1) or any earlier date appointed under sub-section (2) is known as the "prescribed day."

Location of the Principal Seat: The primary location of the High Court of Andhra will be determined by the Governor of Andhra through an order before the prescribed day. If the Legislative Assembly suggests a specific place for the principal seat, the Governor will appoint that place.

SECTION 29 of Andhra State Act, 1953
29. Judges of the Andhra High Court.-
(1) Such of the Judges of the High Court at Madras holding office immediately before the prescribed day as may be determined by the President shall on that day cease to be Judges of the High Court at Madras and become Judges of the High Court of Andhra.
(2) The persons who by virtue of sub-section (1) become Judges of the High Court of Andhra shall, except in the case where any such person is appointed to be the Chief Justice of that High Court, rank in that Court according to the priority of their respective appointments as Judges of the High Court at Madras.
(3) Any person who by virtue of sub-section (1) becomes a Judge of the High Court of Andhra shall, except in the case where a Judge other than the Chief Justice of the High Court at Madras is appointed to be the Chief Justice of the High Court of Andhra, continue to be entitled to receive in respect of time spent on actual service as a Judge of the High Court of Andhra the special pay which he was drawing immediately before the prescribed day under sub-paragraph (2) of paragraph 10 of the Second Schedule to the Constitution.

(1) The High Court of Andhra shall have the like power to approve, admit, enroll, remove and suspend advocates and attorneys and to make rules with respect to advocates and attorneys, as are, under the law in force immediately before the prescribed day, exercisable by the High Court at Madras.

SECTION 38 of Andhra State Act, 1953
38. Transfer of proceedings from Madras High Court to Andhra High Court.-
(1) Except as hereinafter provided, the High Court at Madras shall as from the prescribed day, have no jurisdiction in respect of the State of Andhra.
(2) Such proceedings pending in the High Court at Madras immediately before the prescribed day as are certified, whether before or after that day by the Chief Justice of that High Court having regard to the place of accrual of the cause of action and other circumstances to be proceedings which ought to be heard and decided by the High Court of Andhra shall as soon as may be after such certification be transferred to the High Court of Andhra.
(3) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-sections (1) and (2) of this section or in section 30, but save as hereinafter provided, the High Court at Madras shall have and the High Court of Andhra shall not have, jurisdiction to entertain, hear or dispose of appeals, applications for leave to appeal including leave to appeal to the Supreme Court, applications for review and other proceedings where any such proceedings seek any relief in respect of any order passed by the High Court at Madras before the prescribed day: Provided that if after any such proceedings have been entertained by the High Court at Madras, it appears to the Chief Justice of that High Court that they ought to be transferred to the High Court of Andhra he shall order that they shall be so transferred and such proceedings shall thereupon be transferred accordingly.
(4) Any order made by the High Court at Madras-
(a) before the prescribed day, in any proceedings transferred to the High Court of Andhra by virtue of sub-section (2), or
(b) in any proceedings with respect to which the High Court at Madras retains jurisdiction by virtue of sub-section (3), shall for all purposes have effect, not only as an order of the High Court at Madras, but also as an order made by the High Court of Andhra.

(1) Where before the appointed day the State of Madras had made any contract in the exercise of the executive power of that State for any purposes of the State, then such contract shall-
(a) if such purposes are as from that day-
(i) exclusively purposes of the State of Andhra, or
(ii) partly purposes of the State of Andhra and partly purposes of the State of Mysore and not purposes of the State of Madras as constituted on the appointed day,

and all rights and liabilities which have accrued or may accrue under any such contract shall, to the extent to which they would have been rights or liabilities of the State of Madras as constituted immediately before the appointed day, be rights or liabilities of the State of Andhra, the State of Mysore or the State of Madras, as the case may be.

58. Provisions as to certain pending proceedings.-
(1) Every proceeding pending immediately before the appointed day before a Court (other than the High Court), tribunal, authority or officer-
(a) in any area which on that day falls within the State of Madras or the transferred territory shall, if it is a proceeding relating exclusively to any part of the territories which as from that day are the territories of the State of Andhra, stand transferred to the corresponding court, tribunal, authority or officer in the State of Andhra, or
(b) in any area which on that day falls within the State of Madras or the State of Andhra shall, if it is a proceeding relating exclusively to any part of the transferred territory, stand transferred to the corresponding court, tribunal, authority or officer in the State of Mysore.
(2) If any question arises as to whether any proceeding shall stand transferred under sub-section (1), it shall be referred for the decision of the Chief Justice of the High Court at Madras and his decision shall be final.
(3) In this section-
(a) "proceeding" includes any suit, case or appeal, and
(b) "corresponding court, tribunal, authority or officer" in relation to a State means-
(i) the court, tribunal authority or officer in which the proceeding would have lain if the proceeding had been instituted after the appointed day, or
(ii) in case of doubt, such court, tribunal, authority or officer in the State as may be determined, before the appointed day by the Governor of Madras, and after the appointed day by the Governor or Rajpramukh of that State, to be the corresponding court, tribunal, authority or officer.

61. Provisions relating to the Indian Administrative Service and the Indian Police Service.-
(1) In place of the cadres of the Indian Administrative Service and the Indian Police Service existing in the State of Madras immediately before the appointed day, there shall, as from that day, be two separate cadres, one for the State of Andhra and the other for the State of Madras, in respect of each of the Services.
(2) The President shall, by order, determine the strength and composition of, and the allocation of individual officers, to the said cadres for each of the States of Andhra and Madras.
(3) Every officer allocated under sub-section (2) to the cadre for the State of Andhra who immediately before the appointed day is serving in connection with the affairs of the State of Madras shall,-
(a) if immediately before the appointed day he is holding any post in any area which on that day falls in the State of Andhra, be as from that day, deemed to have been duly appointed to that post by the Government of Andhra; and
(b) if immediately before the appointed day he is not holding any post in any such area, be appointed by the Government of Andhra to a post in connection with the affairs of that State.

Allocation of Officers: Any officer assigned to the cadre for the State of Andhra who is currently working in connection with the affairs of the State of Madras before the appointed day must:

SECTION 63 of Andhra State Act, 1953
63. Provisions relating to other Services.-
(1) The President may by general order require all persons who immediately before the appointed day are serving in connection with the affairs of the State of Madras in the territories specified in sub-section (1) of section 3 or in the transferred territory and who under the terms of their appointments or their conditions of service are not normally liable to be transferred outside the said territories or territory in which they are serving, to serve as from the appointed day in connection with the affairs of the State of Andhra or the State of Mysore, as the case may be, and all allocations so made by the President shall be final.
(2) The President may by special order require any person who is serving immediately before the appointed day in connection with the affairs of the State of Madras and to whom the provisions of sub-section (1) do not apply, to serve in connection with the affairs of the State of Andhra.
(3) Every person who is required to serve under sub-section (1) or sub-section (2) in connection with the affairs of the State of Andhra or the State of Mysore shall,-
(a) if immediately before the appointed day he is holding any post in connection with the affairs of the State of Madras in any area which on that day falls in the State in which he is so required to serve, be deemed as from that day to have been duly appointed to that post by the Government of, or by other appropriate authority in the State concerned in connection with the affairs of that State; and
(b) if immediately before the appointed day he is not holding any post in any such area, be appointed by the Government of, or by other appropriate authority in, the State concerned, to a post in connection with the affairs of that State.
(4) All persons who are required by the President under sub-section (2) to serve in connection with the affairs of the State of Andhra shall be classified by him into the following two categories, namely:-
(i) officers whose allocation to the State of Andhra is final (hereinafter referred to in this section as "allotted officers"), and
(ii) officers required by the President to serve in connection with the affairs of the State of Andhra for a limited period as provided in sub-section (5) (hereinafter referred to in this section as "transferred officers").
(5) The period for which a transferred officer may be required to serve in connection with the affairs of the State of Andhra shall be two years: Provided that the Government of Andhra may return any such officer to the State of Madras at any time before the expiration of the said period after giving three months' notice to him and to the Government of Madras.
(6) An officer shall be classified under sub-section (4) as an allotted officer or a transferred officer according as he is, or is not, in the opinion of the President, suitable for final allotment to the State of Andhra.
(7) A transferred officer shall, during the period he is required to serve in connection with the affairs of the State of Andhra,-
(a) continue to be in the service of the State of Madras and be deemed to be on deputation to the State of Andhra, and
(b) be entitled in addition to the remuneration which he would have drawn if he had continued during such period to serve in connection with the affairs of the State of Madras, to such allowances as the President may by general or special order determine.
(8) A transferred officer shall not be dismissed, removed or reduced in rank except with the previous concurrence of the Government of Madras, and if the Government of Madras does not concur in any such proposal of the Government of Andhra, then the Government of Andhra shall notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (5) return the officer concerned to the State of Madras.
(9) Subject to the provisions of sub-sections (7) and (8), the conditions of service of a transferred officer shall be the same as they would have been if he had continued to serve in connection with the affairs of the State of Madras during the period he is required to serve in connection with the affairs of the State of Andhra.
(10) The foregoing provisions of this section shall not apply in relation to any person to whom the provisions of section 61 or section 62 apply.
simplified_text:
Simplified text: Transfer of Services:

Any person serving in connection with the State of Madras before a certain day may be asked to serve in the State of Andhra or Mysore instead, as directed by the President. This can be either a general requirement affecting everyone or a specific order for certain individuals.

- If an individual is directed to serve in Andhra, they will be considered appointed to their current post in that state.
- If an individual doesn't hold a post in the relevant area before the appointed day, they will be appointed to a suitable post by the State government.
- Individuals transferred to Andhra will be divided into two categories: "allotted officers" with a permanent allotment and "transferred officers" with temporary assignment for up to two years.
- The Andhra government can return a transferred officer to Madras with a three-month notice period.
- A transferred officer's classification as allotted or transferred depends on the President's decision on their suitability.
- During the temporary transfer, officers will be considered on deputation to Andhra and entitled to additional allowances determined by the President.
- Any decision to dismiss, remove, or reduce a transferred officer's rank needs the approval of the Madras government. Failure to get this approval will result in the officer being returned to Madras.
- The terms of service for a transferred officer will be the same as if they were still serving in Madras.
- These rules do not apply to individuals covered under sections 61 or 62.

66. Special provisions with regard to Tungabhadra Project.-
(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act but subject to the provisions of paragraph 12 of the Seventh Schedule, all rights and liabilities of the State of Madras in relation to Tungabhadra Project or the administration thereof shall, on the appointed day, be the rights and liabilities of the States of Andhra and Mysore subject to such adjustments as may be made by agreement entered into by the said States after consultation with the President or if no such agreement is entered into within two years from the appointed day, as the President may by order determine having due regard to the purposes of the Project, and any such order may provide for the management of the Project jointly by the said States or otherwise: Provided that the order so made by the President may be varied by any subsequent agreement entered into by the States of Andhra and Mysore.
(2)An agreement or order referred to in sub-section (1) shall, if there has been an extension or further development of the Project after the appointed day, provide also for the rights and liabilities of the States of Andhra and Mysore in relation to such extension or further development.
(3)The rights and liabilities referred to in sub-sections (1) and (2) shall include-
(a) the rights to receive and to utilise water which may be available for distribution as a result of the Project,
(b) the rights to receive and to utilise the power generated as a result of the Project.
(c) the rights and liabilities in respect of the administration of the Project and the construction, maintenance and operation thereof, but shall not include the rights and liabilities under any contract entered into before the appointed day by the Government of Madras with any person other than Government.
(4) The President may from time to time give such directions as may appear to him to be necessary generally in regard to any of the matters specified in the foregoing provisions of this section and, in particular, for the completion of the Project and its operation and maintenance thereafter: Provided that no such direction shall be issued or have effect after an agreement has been entered into by the States of Andhra and Mysore under sub-section (1) or after an order has been made by the President under that sub-section, whichever is earlier.
(5) In this section, the expression "Tungabhadra Project" or "the Project" means the project agreed to between the Government of Madras and the Government of Hyderabad before the appointed day and, so far as the State of Madras is concerned, intended for the supply and distribution of water from the Tungabhadra river by means of high-level and low level canals to the districts of Bellary, Anantapur, Cuddapah and Kurnool, and for the generation of electric energy, both hydro-electric and thermal, and its transmission and distribution to the said districts and includes any extension or further development after that day of that Project for the said purposes.

The Anti-Apartheid (United Nations Convention) Act, 1981

SECTION 3 of Anti-Hijacking Act, 1982
Anti-Hijacking Act, 1982
CHAPTER II: HIJACKING AND CONNECTED OFFENCES
3. Hijacking
(1)

Whoever on board an aircraft in flight, unlawfully, by force or threat of force

or by any other form of intimidation, seizes or exercises control of that

aircraft, commits the offence of hijacking of such aircraft.
(2)

Whoever attempts to commit any of the acts referred to in sub-section (1) in

relation to any aircraft, or abets the commission of any such act, shall also

be deemed to have committed the offence of hijacking of such aircraft.
(3)

For the purposes of this section, an aircraft shall be deemed to be in flight

at any time from the moment when all its external doors are closed following

embarkation until the moment when any such door is opened for disembarkation,

and in the case of a forced landing, the flight shall be deemed to continue

until the competent authorities of the country in which such forced landing

takes place take over the responsibility for the aircraft and for persons and

property on board.
simplified_text:
Simplified text: Hijacking Offenses:
Hijacking an Aircraft: It is considered hijacking if someone unlawfully takes control of an aircraft in flight using force, threats, or intimidation.

Attempted Hijacking: Trying to hijack an aircraft or helping someone else do it is also treated as hijacking.

Definition of Flight: An aircraft is considered to be in flight from when all its doors are closed after boarding until any door is opened for disembarkation. In case of a forced landing, the flight extends until the authorities of the country where it lands take charge of the aircraft and its occupants.

SECTION 6 of Anti-Hijacking Act, 1982
Anti-Hijacking Act, 1982
6. Jurisdiction
(1)

Subject to the provisions of sub-section (2), where an offence under section 4

or section 5 is committed outside India, the person committing such offence may

be dealt with in respect thereof as if such offence had been committed at any

place within India at which he may be found.
(2)

No court shall take cognizance of an offence punishable under section 4 or

section 5 which is committed outside India unless-
(a) such offence is committed on board an aircraft registered in India;
(b) such offence is committed on board an aircraft which is for the time

being leased without crew to a lessee who has his principal place of business

or where he has no such place of business, his permanent residence in India; or


(c) the alleged offender is a citizen of India or is on board the

aircraft in relation to which such offence is committed when it lands in India

or is found in India.
simplified_text:
Simplified text: Jurisdiction:
1. Offences Outside India: If a person commits an offense under Section 4 or Section 5 outside of India, they can be prosecuted as if the offense had taken place within India wherever they are found.
2. Conditions for Prosecution: A court cannot consider an offense under Section 4 or Section 5 committed outside India unless:
   a. The offense occurs on an Indian-registered aircraft.
   b. The offense happens on an aircraft leased without crew to a lessee with a base in India.
   c. The alleged offender is an Indian citizen or is present on the aircraft when it lands in India.

Definitions:
- Agency: Refers to the National Investigation Agency established under the National Investigation Agency Act, 2008.
- Aircraft: Any aircraft, except military, customs, or police aircraft, regardless of registration.
- Aircraft registered in India: An aircraft currently registered in India.
- Convention country: A nation where the Hague Convention is currently enforced.
- Hague Convention: The Convention for the Suppression of Unlawful Seizure of Aircraft, signed in 1970 at The Hague, including the supplementary Protocol signed in Beijing in 2010.
- Hostage: A passenger, crew member, security personnel, or ground support staff unlawfully seized during aircraft transit or on the ground with the intent to secure specific demands.
- Military aircraft: Any aircraft belonging to naval, military, air force, or other armed forces, including any aircraft under command of armed forces personnel.
- Notification: A notice published in the Official Gazette.
- Security personnel: Individuals deployed by the Central Government or its authorized agencies to ensure civil aviation security against unlawful interference.

Explanation:
Acts of Unlawful Interference:
- Unlawful seizure of aircraft in-flight or on the ground.
- Hostage-taking onboard aircraft or at aerodromes.
- Forceful intrusion onboard aircraft, at aerodromes, or at aeronautical facilities.
- Introducing weapons, explosives, or hazardous substances onboard aircraft with criminal intent.
- Transmitting false information to jeopardize aircraft safety, passenger security, or public safety.

SECTION 3 of Anti-Hijacking Act, 2016
CHAPTER II
HIJACKING AND CONNECTED OFFENCES
3. Hijacking.-
(1) Whoever unlawfully and intentionally seizes or exercises control of an aircraft in service by force or threat thereof, or by coercion, or by any other form of intimidation, or by any technological means, commits the offence of hijacking.
(2) A person shall also be deemed to have committed the offence of hijacking specified in sub-section (1), if, such person-
(a) makes a threat to commit such offence or unlawfully and intentionally causes any person to receive such threat under circumstances which indicate that the threat is credible; or
(b) attempts to commit or abets the commission of such offence; or
(c) organises or directs others to commit such offence or the offence specified in clause (a) or clause (b) above;
(d) participates as an accomplice in such offence or the offence specified in clause (a) or clause (b) above;
(e) unlawfully and intentionally assists another person to evade investigation, prosecution or punishment, knowing that such person has committed any such offence or the offence specified in clause (a) or clause (b) or clause (c) or clause (d) above, or that such person is wanted for criminal prosecution by law enforcement authorities for such an offence or has been sentenced for such an offence.
(3) A person also commits the offence of hijacking, when committed intentionally, whether or not any of the offences specified in sub-section (1) or in clause (a) of sub-section (2) is actually committed or attempted, either or both of the following:-
(a) agreeing with one or more other persons to commit an offence specified in sub-section (1) or in clause (a) of sub-section (2), involving an act undertaken by one of the participants in furtherance of the agreement; or
(b) contributing in any manner to the commission of an offence specified in sub-section (1) or in clause (a) of sub-section (2) by a group of persons acting with a common purpose and such contribution shall either-
(i) be made with the aim of furthering the general criminal activity or purpose of the group, where such activity or purpose involves the commission of such an offence; or
(ii) be made in the knowledge of the intention of the group to commit such offence.
(4) For the purposes of this Act, an aircraft shall be considered to be "in service" from the beginning of the pre-flight preparation of the aircraft by ground personnel or by the crew for a specific flight until twenty-four hours after any landing and in the case of a forced landing, the flight shall be deemed to continue until the competent authorities take over the responsibility for the aircraft and for persons and property on board.
simplified_text:
Simplified text: Hijacking Offences:
1. Hijacking: Taking control of an aircraft using force, threats, coercion, intimidation, or technology is considered hijacking.
- This includes making credible threats, attempting, helping others commit, organizing, or assisting someone evade punishment for hijacking-related offenses.
2. Agreement or Contribution: Agreeing to commit hijacking with others or contributing to a group's criminal activity that includes hijacking will also be considered hijacking.
- An aircraft is considered "in service" from pre-flight preparation until 24 hours after landing, or until authorities take control after a forced landing.

Simplified text: Jurisdiction:
1. If a person commits a crime under section 3 or 5 outside India, they can be prosecuted in India where they are found.
2. A Court in India can only hear cases of crimes under section 3 or 5 committed outside India if:
   - The offence happens in India.
   - The offence is on or against an Indian-registered aircraft.
   - The offence is on an aircraft that lands in India with the offender still on board.
   - The offence involves an aircraft leased to someone based in India.
   - The offence involves or affects an Indian citizen.
   - The offence involves a stateless person residing in India.
   - The offender is in India but not extradited according to section 11.

SECTION 18 of Anti-Hijacking Act, 2016
18. Powers of investigating officers to seize or attach property.-
(1) Where any officer, referred to in section 6, while conducting an inquiry or investigation has a reason to believe that any property, movable or immovable, or both, is relatable to the commission of the offence in relation to which such inquiry or investigation is being conducted, is likely to be concealed, transferred or dealt with in any manner which will result in disposal of such property, he may make an order for seizing such property and where it is not practicable to seize such property, he may make an order of attachment directing that such property shall not be transferred or otherwise dealt with, except with the prior permission of the officer making such order, and a copy of such order shall be served on the person concerned.
(2) Any order made under sub-section (1) shall have no effect unless the said order is confirmed by an order of the Designated Court, within a period of forty-eight hours of its being made.
(3) The Designated Court may either confirm or revoke the order of seizure or attachment referred to in sub-section (2).
(4) Notwithstanding the confirmation of the order by the Designated Court under sub-section (3), any person aggrieved by the order of attachment made under sub-section (1), may make an application to the Designated Court for revocation of said order within a period of thirty days from the date of confirmation of the order under sub-section (3).

Simplified text: SEIZURE OR ATTACHMENT OF PROPERTY

When investigating an offense, officers have the power to seize or attach any property they believe is connected to the crime and at risk of being hidden, moved, or disposed of. If seizing the property is not possible, they can order it to be attached, meaning it cannot be transferred or dealt with without permission. The person involved must be informed of this order.

This order is temporary and needs to be confirmed by the Designated Court within 48 hours to remain valid. The court can either confirm or cancel the seizure or attachment order.

Even after confirmation by the court, a person affected by the attachment order can request the court to cancel it within 30 days from the confirmation date.

13. Power of Central Government to carry on the business of selling antiquities to the exclusion of others.-
(1) If the Central Government is of opinion that with a view to conserving antiquities or in the public interest it is necessary or expedient so to do, it may, by notification in the Official Gazette, declare that with effect on and from such date as may be specified in the notification, the Central Government or any authority or agency authorised by the Central Government in this behalf shall alone be entitled to carry on the business of selling or offering for sale of antiquities.
(2) On the issue of a notification under sub-section (1),-
(a) it shall not be lawful for any person, authority or agency, other than the Central Government or any authority or agency authorized by the Central Government, to carry on the business of selling or offering for sale any antiquity on and from the date specified therein;
(b) the provisions of this Act, in so far as they relate to the licensing of persons carrying on the business of selling or offering for sale of antiquities shall cease to have effect except as respects things done or omitted to be done before such cesser of operation and section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 (10 of 1897) shall apply upon such cesser of operation as if those provisions had been repealed by a Central Act:
Provided that every licence granted under section 8 and in force on the date aforesaid shall, notwithstanding that the period specified therein has not expired, cease to be in force.
(3) Every person whose licence has ceased to be in force under the proviso to clause (b) of sub-section (2) shall, within such period, in such form and in such manner as may be prescribed, make a declaration before the licensing officer of all the antiquities in his ownership, control or possession immediately before the date specified in the notification issued under sub-section (1).

SECTION 19 of Antiquities and Art Treasures Act, 1972
19. Power of Central Government to compulsorily acquire antiquities and art treasures.-
(1) If the Central Government is of opinion that it is desirable to preserve any antiquity or art treasure in a public place, that Government may make an order for the compulsory acquisition of such antiquity or art treasure.
(2) On the making of an order under sub-section (1) the Collector of the district in which such antiquity or art treasure is kept shall give notice to the owner thereof intimating him of the decision of the Central Government to acquire the same and it shall be lawful for the Collector to take possession of such antiquity or art treasure, for which purpose the Collector may use such force as may be necessary.
(3) Where the owner of any antiquity or art treasure the possession of which has been taken over by the Collector under sub-section (2) objects to the taking over of such possession, he may, within a period of thirty days from the date on which such possession was taken over, make a representation to the Central Government putting forth his objections: Provided that the Central Government may entertain the representation after the expiry of the said period of thirty days, if it is satisfied that the owner of such antiquity or art treasure was prevented by sufficient cause from making the representation in time.
(4) On receipt of any representation under sub-section (3), the Central Government, after making such inquiry as it deems fit and after giving to the objector an opportunity of being heard in the matter, shall, within a period of ninety days from the date of receipt of the representation, either rescind or confirm the order made by it under sub-section (1).
(5) Where any order made by the Central Government under sub-section (1) is rescinded under sub-section (4) the antiquity or art treasure shall be returned to the owner thereof without delay and at the expense of the Central Government.
(6) Where the order made by the Central Government under sub-section (1) is confirmed under sub-section (4) the antiquity or art treasure shall vest in the Central Government with effect from the date on which the possession thereof has been taken over by the Collector under sub-section (2).
(7) The power of compulsory acquisition conferred by this section shall not extend to any object, being an antiquity or art treasure, used for bona fide religious observances.
Explanation.-In this section, "public place" means any place which is open to the use of the public, whether on payment of fees or not, or whether it is actually used by the public or not.
simplified_text:
Simplified text: Acquisition of Antiquities and Art Treasures: The Central Government can acquire antiquities or art treasures in public places if it is deemed necessary to preserve them. The process involves the following steps:

1. Acquisition Order: If the Central Government decides to acquire an antiquity or art treasure, the Collector of the district where it is located will inform the owner and take possession using necessary force.

2. Owner's Objections: If the owner disagrees with the possession being taken, they can make a written objection to the Central Government within thirty days. The Government may still consider the objection after this period under certain circumstances.

3. Central Government's Decision: After receiving an objection, the Central Government will investigate and hold a hearing. Within ninety days, they will confirm or revoke the acquisition order.

4. Result of Decision: If the order is revoked, the antiquity or art treasure will be returned to the owner at the Government's expense. If the order is confirmed, ownership transfers to the Central Government upon possession by the Collector.

5. Exception: The Government cannot acquire objects used for genuine religious practices.

Note: "Public place" refers to any location accessible to the public, whether or not fees are required for entry or if it is actively used by the public.

Simplified text:

Compensation for Acquired Antiquities:
When an antiquity or art treasure is acquired under section 19, compensation must be paid. The amount of compensation is determined as follows:
If agreement can be reached on the amount, it is paid as per the agreement.
If no agreement is reached, an arbitrator appointed by the Central Government with legal expertise will decide on the fair compensation.
An expert on the nature of the acquired item can be nominated by the Central Government, and the affected party can also nominate an assessor.
The arbitrator will hear both sides and make a fair award based on the circumstances and factors outlined in subsection (2).
In case of disputes over compensation recipients, the arbitrator will decide and allocate the compensation accordingly.
The Arbitration Act, 1940, does not apply to arbitrations under this section.

Factors Considered in Compensation:
The arbitrator will consider the following factors in determining compensation:
The antiquity or art treasure's historical significance and belonging period.
The artistic, aesthetic, historical, architectural, archaeological, or anthropological importance of the item.
The rarity of the antiquity or art treasure.
Other relevant matters related to the dispute.

Arbitration Powers:
The appointed arbitrator has the powers of a Civil Court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, including:
Summoning and examining witnesses under oath.
Requiring the production of documents.
Accepting evidence through affidavits.
Obtaining public records.
Issuing commissions for witness examination.

25. Penalty.-
(1) If any person, himself or by any other person on his behalf, exports or attempts to export any antiquity or art treasure in contravention of section 3, he shall, without prejudice to any confiscation or penalty to which he may be liable under the provisions of the Customs Act, 1962 (52 of 1962) as applied by section 4, be punishable with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than six months but which may extend to three years and with fine.

(3) if any person prevents any licensing officer from inspecting any record, photograph or register maintained under section 10 or prevents any officer authorized by the Central Government under sub-section (1) of section 23 from entering into or searching any place under that sub-section, he shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine, or with both.

28. Offences by companies.-
(1) Where an offence under this Act has been committed by a company, every person who at the time the offence was committed was in charge of, or was responsible to, the company for the conduct of the business of the company, as well as the company, shall be deemed to be guilty of the offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly: Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall render any such person liable to any punishment under this Act if he proves that the offence was committed without his knowledge or that he exercised all due diligence to prevent the commission of such offence.
(2) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), where an offence under this Act has been committed with the consent or connivance of, or is attributable to, any neglect on the part of any director, manager, secretary or other officer of the company, such director, manager, secretary or other officer shall also be deemed to be guilty of that offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly.

(a) "company" means any body corporate and includes a firm or other association of individuals; and
(b) "director", in relation to a firm, means a partner in the firm.

Apprenticeship Council.
(8)(a) Recurring costs

(including the cost of stipends) incurred by an employer in connection with

basic training, imparted to trade apprentices other than those referred to in

Government and beyond that limit, by the employer alone; and
(b) Recurring costs

(c) Recurring costs

Simplified text: Practical Training for Apprentices:

Monitoring: The Central Apprenticeship Adviser or authorized personnel must have access to apprentices for testing their work and ensuring proper training. State-level advisers must also be given access for apprentices under them.

Basic Training: Apprentices who haven't had institutional training need to undergo a basic training course before starting practical training. Large employers need to provide basic training separately in their workshop or a designated building.

Training Requirement:
- Large Employers: Employers with 500 or more workers should provide basic training on-site. The government may provide loans for setting up separate training facilities.
- Small Employers: Those with fewer than 500 workers should send apprentices to government training institutes.

Training Syllabus: The syllabus and equipment for training must be approved by the Central Government in consultation with the Central Apprenticeship Council.

Cost Sharing: Recurring costs for basic training for trade apprentices are shared between employers and the government based on the number of workers. Costs for graduate or technician apprentices are shared between the employer and the Central Government based on set limits.
